newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Sense of deja vu in Russia as Yeltsin fights Lebed.
newsitem.headline: Sense of deja vu in Russia as Yeltsin fights Lebed.

text.p: There was a distinct sense of deja vu when Russian President Boris Yeltsin signed a decree sacking Alexander Lebed as his security chief in an act of high drama captured by the television cameras.
Yeltsin should take heed. Humiliated by then Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev in 1987, he fought back to become Russia's president and belittle Gorbachev in his turn.
"He (Lebed) is like the Boris Yeltsin of 1987," Boris Nemtsov, a popular provincial governor, told Interfax news agency on Friday, one day after Lebed's dismissal.
Yeltsin has been on both ends of it. He has humbled others and been humbled by others during the years of turmoil which have overstrained his heart.
In 1985, Gorbachev brought Yeltsin to Moscow and made him a junior member of the ruling politburo.
Two years later, in an act viewed by Gorbachev as treacherous ingratitude, Yeltsin challenged him over the pace of reforms and paid the price by losing his post.
Humiliation came from all sides. The phrase "Boris, you are wrong" from arch foe and Communist Party ideologue Yegor Ligachev became famous in Russia but was the softest he was to hear.
To use a Russian saying, only the lazy did not kick Yeltsin. It was tortuous and brought Yeltsin down with heart problems and a nervous breakdown, according to his autobiography.

Most of the Russian media loyal to the Kremlin found it hard to conceal its delight over Lebed's sacking. "The swan has flown away," said the newspaper Rossiiskiye Vesti on Friday in a gleeful pun on Lebed's name, which means swan.
But Yeltsin's disgrace in 1987 was the start of his rise to power. He first became a leader of the emerging political opposition, then head of the Russian parliament.
In 1990, in a typically theatrical move, Yeltsin walked out of the Communist Party at a congress. His public popularity soared.
In June 1991, despite opposition by Gorbachev, Yeltsin won a landslide election victory to become president of the Russian Federation, then part of the Soviet Union.
The position allowed him to start paying back his "debts". An attempted hardline coup against Gorbachev in August 1991 gave him a perfect opportunity to do so.
The coup failed on August 21. Two days later, Gorbachev attended a session of the Russian parliament and Yeltsin was ready and waiting.

Before millions of television viewers, clearly relishing the moment, Yeltsin produced a decree temporarily banning the Russian republic's Communist Party and, ignoring Gorbachev's feeble attempts to protest, said:
"On a lighter note, shall we now sign a decree suspending the activities of the Russian Communist Party."
Yeltsin then signed it with a flourish.
On the first day of the coup, August 19, Yeltsin met Lebed whom he described in his book as "a straightforward man, who put his military officer's sense of honour above everything".

On Thursday, Yeltsin, re-elected with Lebed's help in July for another four years, summoned all his energy to go on television to denounce Lebed from the sanatorium where he is preparing for heart surgery.
He also criticised Alexander Korzhakov, his former bodygguard and close confidant, whom he sacked in June.
"They are birds of a feather. Two generals," he said with contempt and clearly-felt emotion. He went on to read out his decree sacking Lebed and then signed it for the cameras.
Lebed, already the most trusted politician in the country according to a recent opinion poll, is now free to pursue his political ambition to succeed Yeltsin.
"In general, we have a clear-cut and ready candidate who has been purged from the Kremlin nine years after Boris Yeltsin was expelled from the politburo," said the liberal Sevodnya daily newspaper.
Liberal parliament deputy Sergei Yushenkov seemed to disagree. "History repeats itself only as a farce," he said.
